findings: Lateral projection radiograph of the knee joint
Distal femur and proximal tibia and fibula are visualized

Two curvilinear ossific densities are seen anterior and lateral to the lateral femoral condyle, appearing as smooth, well-corticated bony fragments projecting lateral to the joint; they are separate from the main femoral condyle
The joint space appears relatively preserved
No gross fracture line is identified in the distal femur, proximal tibia, or fibula
Soft tissue swelling is not clearly identified on this projection
The patella is partially visible superimposed on the femoral condyles in this lateral projection
No obvious periosteal reaction or aggressive bony lesion is identified
differential: Osteochondral loose bodies (intra-articular or para-articular ossified fragments, most likely related to osteochondritis dissecans or prior osteochondral injury)
Pellegrini-Stieda lesion or post-traumatic periarticular ossification/avulsion fragment at the lateral collateral ligament complex
Fabella variant or bipartite fabella (normal sesamoid bone in the lateral head of gastrocnemius, though the morphology and apparent doubling suggest a variant or fracture)
anatomyConcerns: The two ossific densities lateral to the lateral femoral condyle could represent a fabella (normal sesamoid) that appears bipartite or fractured; a true bipartite fabella is a recognized anatomic variant but should be distinguished from fracture or loose body
Projection is lateral but with slight obliquity, which may cause the two fragments to appear separated when they could be superimposed structures
No markers or laterality indicators are visible to confirm which knee (left or right) is imaged
